items.title: Jimmy Owens interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001
items.q: Being Billie Holiday, being Bessie Smith and Louis Armstrong. There were no hotels, there were no places to eat.

ctx.x: The association of jazz with drugs and so forth is pretty documented. Has it changed over the years? Has it gotten better or worse?

Oh most definitely. It’s gotten better because life in America has gotten better. As we pinpointed racism a little more and made things better for African American people, narcotics stopped a little bit in the jazz musician — a lot I should say — in the jazz musician community. It’s really difficult being in Duke Ellington’s band and traveling through the south in the 30s. There were no hotels. Being Billie Holiday, being Bessie Smith and Louis Armstrong. There were no hotels, there were no places to eat. I mean…
Do you think there’s a misdirected opinion with some of the European musicians that the narcotics help you to play this?
